subdivision.heading: General Rule, Considerations and Court Authority

operative_text.controlling:
10.34(1)  The Court may order an assessment of costs by an
assessment officer and may give directions to the assessment
officer about the assessment.
(2)  The Court must keep a record on the court file of a direction
(a) given to an assessment officer,
(b) requested by a party and refused by the Court, or
(c) requested by a party that the Court declines to make but
leaves to an assessment officer’s discretion.

BOOK_A.title: Court-ordered Assessment of Costs
BOOK_A.commentary:
On when costs are payable, see the Crouser case.⁷
A chambers judge used R.9.12 to give full costs of a suit, even after entry of a formal summary
judgment which had only given costs of that application.⁸

Where a consent order awards solicitor-client costs, the assessment ofﬁcer cannot cut them
in half.¹

footnotes.text: Quite similar to previous R.601(4). It was ﬁrst enacted by Alta. Reg.152/98.
Crouser-Reymon v. Tawa Dev.2010 ABQB 166, 491 AR 301.
Alta. Treas. Br. v.1401057 Alta.2013 ABQB 748, 579 AR 152.

BOOK_C.title: Court-ordered assessment of costs

commentary.text:
Courts have discretion to direct that an assessment of costs be conducted by an assessment officer, and may give specific directions for the assessment — such as ensuring that a bill of costs includes only costs and legal expenses incurred with respect to a particular proceeding.  Condominium Plan No. 052 6233 v. Seehra, [2014] A.J. No. 1059, 2014 ABQB 588 at para. 29 (Alta. Q.B.).
Directing an assessment is useful when actual legal expenses are used as the basis of party and party costs. McAllister v. Calgary (City), [2021] A.J. No. 109, 2021 ABCA 25 at paras. 46, 66 (Alta. C.A.); Patel v. Chief Medical Supplies Ltd., [2021] A.J. No. 625, 2021 ABQB 355 at paras. 130-131 (Alta. Q.B.).
Subdivision 2: ASSESSMENT OF COSTS BY ASSESSMENT OFFICER
